title: 3-Read Friday #106: Working Memory, Lesson Principles, and AI Evidence in K-12
author: Craig Barton
summary: 3-Read Friday #106 leads with Efrat Furst reconceiving working memory not as a limited container to avoid overloading, but as an active process in which the depth and structure of prior knowledge determines what new learning can actually be built. Hali Hughes then argues that lesson principles only improve pupils' experience when leaders treat implementation not as a one-off launch event but as a sustained, structured architecture -- translating abstract beliefs into specific routines, supported by coaching, aligned systems, and the discipline to do fewer things more deeply. The issue closes with a Stanford Scale Initiative report finding that despite rapid growth in AI-in-education research, rigorous causal evidence remains thin, with early findings suggesting tool design and pedagogical guardrails -- not AI access alone -- determine whether students develop durable learning or mere tool-dependent performance. Barton calls the Furst piece the best post he has ever read on working memory, signalling unusually strong endorsement.
points: Furst reframes working memory as an active process shaped by the depth and structure of prior knowledge, not a fixed-capacity container to be protected from overload -- a genuinely different model of what limits learning.

Hughes's implementation argument: lesson principles only change practice when leadership treats rollout as sustained architecture -- coaching, aligned systems, and doing fewer things more deeply -- rather than a single launch event.

The Stanford Scale Initiative finding is a caution against AI-in-education hype: causal evidence is still thin, and tool design plus pedagogical guardrails, not mere access to AI, determine whether learning is durable or just performance.
Barton's unusually strong personal endorsement of the Furst piece ('the best post I have ever read on working memory') signals it as required reading, not just a routine pick.
